patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch addresses a bug in the compat bitmap read for get_mempolicy() calls on 32-bit systems, where it can read past the kernel's stack nodemask due to an incorrect calculation of the number of bytes to copy. The fix bounds the compat bitmap read by MAX_NUMNODES and maintains existing behavior when the kernel nodemask is large enough.

review_comments.author: David Hildenbrand (Arm)
review_comments.summary: LGTM, but suggested reworking compat_put_bitmap() to handle bits instead of words for better alignment with copy_to_user().

review_comments.author: Arnd Bergmann
review_comments.summary: Identified an off-by-one error in the calculation of copy bytes, which affects both native and compat syscalls. Suggested fixing this by aligning maxnode to 64 bits instead of 64 words.

review_comments.author: Arnd Bergmann
review_comments.summary: Raised concerns about the ABI implications of changing the behavior for 32-bit userspace asking for maxnum that results in an odd number of 32-bit words.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Tue, Nov 17, 2026, at 13:44, Arnd Bergmann wrote:
> On Tue, Nov 17, 2026, at 11:19, Gregory Price (Meta) wrote:
>> A 32-bit get_mempolicy() call can read past the kernel's stack nodemask.
>> With 64 possible nodes and maxnode=65, copy_nodes_to_user() computes an
>> eight-byte copy, but compat_put_bitmap() reads two native words.
>
> I don't quite follow the explanation yet:
>
> if maxnode=65, shouldn't that result in copying 16 bytes on x86-64
> and 12 bytes on compat mode?
>
> It looks like compat mode adjusts the wrong variable and we should
> be doing this instead:
>
> diff --git a/mm/mempolicy.c b/mm/mempolicy.c
> index 6d662a9a8c74..f9a7be9f4432 100644
> --- a/mm/mempolicy.c
> +++ b/mm/mempolicy.c
> @@ -1749,12 +1749,12 @@ static int get_nodes(nodemask_t *nodes, const 
> unsigned long __user *nmask,
>  static int copy_nodes_to_user(unsigned long __user *mask, unsigned 
> long maxnode,
>  			      nodemask_t *nodes)
>  {
> -	unsigned long copy = ALIGN(maxnode-1, 64) / 8;
> +	unsigned long copy = ALIGN(maxnode-1, BITS_PER_LONG) / 8;

I guess this would be an ABI change for 32-bit userspace asking for
maxnum that results in an odd number of 32-bit words. The man
page documents this as "The value specified by maxnode is always
rounded to a multiple of sizeof(unsigned long)*8", while the
code here has always rounded it up to a multiple of 64 in
both native (no longer supported on 32-bit) and compat syscalls.

numactl (1) always uses 128 or 2048 bit masks and won't notice
it either way, so we can possibly change the ABI here and
do what the man page says, or keep the current behavior and update
the man page.

It looks like the other part of the problem is the off-by-one
error: the "ALIGN(maxnode-1, 64) / 8" rounds down maxnode=65
to copy=8 which is the same as nbytes, but the compat_put_bitmap()
treats it as a 65-bit map that needs 96 bytes. 

This means we have a related bug on native syscalls as well:
asking for a 65 bit mask in mempolicy only returns 8 bytes
without clearing the next word like it would for a 66 bit mask.
If we just fix the off-by-one and keep the 64 bit alignment
(with a manpage update), the version below be should be sufficient.

   Arnd

--- a/mm/mempolicy.c
+++ b/mm/mempolicy.c
@@ -1749,13 +1749,10 @@ static int get_nodes(nodemask_t *nodes, const unsigned long __user *nmask,
 static int copy_nodes_to_user(unsigned long __user *mask, unsigned long maxnode,
                              nodemask_t *nodes)
 {
-       unsigned long copy = ALIGN(maxnode-1, 64) / 8;
+       unsigned long copy = ALIGN(maxnode, 64) / 8;
        unsigned int nbytes = BITS_TO_LONGS(nr_node_ids) * sizeof(long);
        bool compat = in_compat_syscall();
 
-       if (compat)
-               nbytes = BITS_TO_COMPAT_LONGS(nr_node_ids) * sizeof(compat_long_t);
-
        if (copy > nbytes) {
                if (copy > PAGE_SIZE)
                        return -EINVAL;

patches_reviewed.subject: Re: [PATCH] mm/mempolicy: fix copy_nodes_to_user() for odd inputs
patches_reviewed.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug in the Linux kernel's memory policy module where the function copy_nodes_to_user() would read and write one extra byte from/to user space when maxnode - 1 is a multiple of 32, leading to a stack over-read and leak. The fix involves converting maxnode to a bit count on entry to copy_nodes_to_user() and get_nodes(), ensuring that both the native and compat paths get the same size for the node mask. This patch addresses an issue introduced in commit e130242dc351 and is intended to be backported to stable kernels.

review_comments.author: Arnd Bergmann
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Arnd Bergmann noted that renaming maxnode to nbits in copy_nodes_to_user() makes it harder to backport patches to stable kernels, and suggested doing a minimal fix first.

Reviewer noted that the nbytes assignment in get_nodes() has no benefit for NODES_SHIFT >= 6 and suggested dropping it, assuming it was a mistake when introducing the bug.
review_comments.raw_body:
I like the renaming as a cleanup, though it does make it a little
harder to backport to stable kernels from context changes, maybe
it's better to do do the minimal fix first.

---

It fixes the bug, but I'd drop the nbytes= assignment here, as it
has no benefit: The only configurations where nbytes actually gets
a different value is for NODES_SHIFT<6, but as the on-stack
bitmask is still a 64-bit word here, the only difference is whether
the extra zeroes come from memset() or compat_put_bitmap().

I assume that when I introduced this bug, I simply confused which of
the two variables needed to be adjusted.

      Arnd

patches_reviewed.subject: Re: [RFC PATCH v4 00/10] add provenance time (ptime)
patches_reviewed.patch_summary: This patch series proposes to add a 'provenance time' (ptime) field to the Linux kernel, which would track when an inode's metadata was last updated. However, it seems that managing this field in the kernel is complex and may require userland intervention. A simpler approach suggested by Jeff Layton is to make the existing 'btime' (birth time) settable from userland or to store the provenance time as an extended attribute (xattr).

review_comments.author: koraynilay
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer noted that managing provenance time (ptime) in the kernel is challenging and suggested revisiting the decision to make btime settable from userland, or alternatively tracking ptime as an xattr.

Reviewer koraynilay clarified the meaning of various inode timestamps, explaining that btime is 'inode birth/creation time', ctime is 'inode change time', mtime is 'file content change/modification time', and ptime would be 'file content creation time'.

Reviewer noted that setting an immutable inode creation time (ctime) is necessary even if btime is made settable, and suggested tracking the new timestamp in an xattr instead of adding a new per-inode field.

Reviewer noted that userland xattrs have limitations (e.g., don't work on symlinks) and suggested using them instead of adding a new inode timestamp, citing their own experience with fully userspace xattrs for backups.

reviewer expressed concerns that the proposed solution to track provenance time is overly complex and suggested a simpler alternative of tracking it in an xattr, citing samba's behavior as an example
review_comments.raw_body:
Hello and thanks for replying,

On Wed Nov 18, 2026 at 12:53 AM CET, Jeff Layton wrote:

---

|-----\_-----------------|-----------|
  |       \_      change/  |   birth/  |
  |         \_ modification|  creation |
  |           \------------|-----------|
  | inode time |   ctime   |   btime   |
  |------------|-----------|-----------|
  | file time  |   mtime   |   ptime   |
  |------------|-----------|-----------|
  
("file" as in "the concept of this file", I'd say "file content" but
that would be incorrect for symlinks)

so ctime is "inode change time", btime is "inode birth/creation time",
while mtime is "file content change/modification time" and ptime would
be "file content creation time" (same as Window's or MacOS's creation
time).

Does this make more sense?

---

Originally I just wanted to have btime settable, yes, and if btime was
settable I wouldn't have made this RFC PATCH either, but after reading
the already existing discussions about it, I can understand having an
"immutable inode creation time", like ctime exists, so even after making
btime settable, a new timestamp would be necessary anyway (e.g. for the
people who want btime to exist as a forensics timestamp).

---

(This is copied and adapted from [2])

I actually have been using fully userspace xattrs[1] for a few months,
mostly for backups, and it "works"; but last month I wanted to merge 2
FSs (and have another merge I have to do), so I ran [1] on all files and
then compared all metadata/data between source and destination and
noticed there were quite a lot of files that didn't have the xattr set.
So I looked online and learned that xattrs only work on regular
files/directories, not on symlinks or anything else (and the missing
ones were of symlinks).
This is what prompted me to search more if anyone had already proposed a
new timestamp (instead of making btime settable) and found the email
thread from april linked in the cover letter, which gave me the excuse
to finally work on a proper patch.

---

So yeah while I do agree it touches a lot of code that could create
problems, IMO this is the best solution and it would complete files'
timestamps like other OSs have (and this, I think, is necessary for
both backup/archival and migrations).

Thanks,
koraynilay

[1]: https://github.com/koraynilay/btime-to-xattr
[2]: https://lore.kernel.org/DMGS4KQLY24Q.14MUTR6U93GIC@gmail.com/

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 1/4] mm/huge_memory: scale thp_underused() to the folio size
series_items.patch_summary: This patch updates the thp_underused() function to be aware of the size of a folio, rather than just PMD-sized folios. It scales the khugepaged_max_ptes_none threshold proportionally to the number of pages in the folio, ensuring that the same fraction of zero-filled pages is tolerated for any folio size. This change will prevent issues when collapsing mTHP orders and splitting folios. The patch has no functional changes for PMD-sized folios, as their nr_pages value remains HPAGE_PMD_NR.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 2/4] mm/huge_memory: don't queue folios when underused splitting is inactive
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the Linux kernel's huge memory management to prevent anonymous PMD-sized folios from being queued for underused splitting when the system is configured to tolerate any number of zero-filled pages. This change is made by factoring out a check into a new function, thp_underused_never(), which is used in both deferred_split_folio() and thp_underused(). The patch also addresses an issue where folios that were already scanned are not requeued when the sysctl changes.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 3/4] mm/huge_memory: add a per-order counter for underused splits
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a per-order counter for underused huge page splits in the Linux kernel's memory management system. The existing thp_underused_split_page counter only counts PMD-sized folios, but this change introduces a new split_underused stat that tracks underused splits of all sizes. This is done to match the behavior of other THP split stats and provide more accurate information about huge page usage. The patch makes changes to several files, including Documentation/admin-guide/mm/transhuge.rst, include/linux/huge_mm.h, and mm/huge_memory.c.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 4/4] mm: add anonymous mTHP folios to the deferred split list
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds anonymous mTHP folios to the deferred split list, allowing them to be split when under memory pressure and reclaiming unused space. This is necessary because current behavior doesn't add these folios to the list, causing memory regressions on systems with large THPs. The patch introduces a minimum size of 2M for mTHP folios to be queued for underused splitting, which can be adjusted later if needed. It also maintains backwards compatibility by exempting PMD-sized folios from this minimum size.

version_history.subject: [PATCH] mm/compaction: do not skip the free scanner's periodic lock drop

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug in the Linux kernel's compaction module, which is responsible for compacting free memory pages. The issue arises when scanning compound pages or high-order free pages with a stride above one, causing the lock to be held and interrupts disabled without periodic drops. To fix this, the patch counts probes instead of page frames and checks every COMPACT_CLUSTER_MAX probes for fatal signals, ensuring that the lock is dropped periodically.

review_comments.author: SJ Park
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer noted that the patch's change to count probes instead of pfns may lead to an issue where the scan does not always land on a multiple of COMPACT_CLUSTER_MAX, and requested clarification.

Reviewer suggested leaving certain lines of code unchanged without expressing a strong opinion or blocking the patch
